title: Development of β‐Lactamase‐Labeling Nanoparticle for 19 F NMR/Fluorescence Detection
authors: Hiroto Fukuda; Masafumi Minoshima; Kazuya Kikuchi
matched_keywords: fluorescence imaging; molecular imaging; fluorescent probe
abstract: β‐Lactamase is involved in the emergence and spread of antimicrobial‐resistant bacteria by hydrolyzing β‐lactam antibiotics, and it is widely used as a genetically encoded reporter in biological studies. Dual‐modal 19 F NMR/fluorescent probes are attractive tools for molecular imaging; however, developing a probe that supports both modalities for detecting β‐lactamase remains challenging. In this study, we developed a silica nanoparticle‐based nanoprobe (FLAME‐DBO) for 19 F NMR/fluorescence detection of β‐lactamase. FLAME‐DBO was synthesized by encapsulating perfluorocarbon in the core, conjugating fluorophores in the shell, and modifying diazabicyclooctanes (DBO) on the surface for labeling β‐lactamase. The FLAME‐based dual‐modal nanoprobe can selectively label and accumulate in mammalian cells and Escherichia coli expressing β‐lactamase on the membrane surface. This nanoprobe offers a promising tool for detecting β‐lactamase using 19 F NMR and fluorescence imaging in living cells.

title: Multi-level spinal cord stimulation to treat pain, orthostatic intolerance and autonomic symptoms in postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome: a pilot case series
authors: Cristian Rizea; José Paz-Solís; Que Doan; Ismael Huertas
abstract: Abstract Background Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is a chronic and often disabling disorder characterized by orthostatic intolerance and excessive heart-rate increase. POTS may be accompanied by chronic pain and other autonomic symptoms that further impair quality of life. We report a pilot case series of patients with painful POTS and persistent symptoms despite conventional medical management treated with spinal cord stimulation (SCS). Methods Five patients with painful POTS underwent implantation of three percutaneous SCS leads (two thoracic leads [T9-T12] and one cervical lead [C5-T1]). Assessments were performed before and after SCS over 12 months and included pain (VAS), autonomic symptoms using the Boston Autonomic Symptom​ Questionnaire (BASQ), health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using SF-36v2, and head-up tilt testing with assessment of the orthostatic heart-rate response (ΔHR). Results Pain was substantially reduced after SCS (VAS, 8.0 to 2.6; p = 0.003). Postural tachycardia also decreased, with reductions in mean ΔHR from 32.7 to 11.2 beats/min ( p = 0.05). Autonomic symptom burden decreased by approximately 50% (BASQ, 45.5 to 22.9; p = 0.01), with improvements in orthostatic intolerance (7.3 to 1.7; p = 0.02) and selected cardiorespiratory, genitourinary, and gastrointestinal symptoms. HRQoL improved, particularly physical functioning (15 to 66; p p = 0.002), with additional improvements in bodily pain and vitality. Heart rate variability analyses showed changes consistent with improved autonomic regulation during orthostatic stress. Conclusions In this pilot case series, multi-level SCS was associated with improvements in pain, orthostatic tachycardia, autonomic symptoms, and quality of life in patients with POTS. The rapid improvement in orthostatic heart-rate responses and preliminary hemodynamic observations support further investigation of SCS as a neuromodulatory approach for POTS.

title: Indanonalkene Photoluminescent Platform: From Reaction-Encoded Fluorescence to Adaptive Soft Materials and Chemical Biology
authors: Wenhai Bian; Ke Wei; Haiqiao Huang; Xiaolong Sun
abstract: Conspectus Dynamic covalent chemistry provides a powerful framework for constructing adaptive molecular and materials systems, while fluorescence offers a sensitive and noninvasive means to visualize chemical processes in real time. In most reported systems, however, these two components are combined only modularly: fluorophores are appended as passive reporters, and the resulting optical signals are only indirectly related to the underlying bond-forming or bond-breaking events. This separation limits the ability of fluorescence to faithfully encode chemical state, transformation pathway, and reaction history. In this Account, we describe a unified platform based on indanonalkene-derived conjugate acceptors in which chemical reactivity and fluorescence are intrinsically coupled within the same molecular scaffold. These acceptors undergo nucleophilic addition, conjugate substitution, intramolecular cyclization, and elimination reactions that directly reorganize the π-conjugation pathway and alter excited-state decay. Consequently, otherwise weakly emissive or nonemissive intermediates are converted into fluorescent products, allowing covalent transformations to be reported stoichiometrically and in real time. Three complementary photophysical modes underpin this platform. Cyclization-regulated fluorescence emission (CRFE) arises when reaction-induced ring formation rigidifies the scaffold and suppresses nonradiative relaxation. Displacement-induced fluorescence emission (DIFE) results from substitution of sulfur-based leaving groups by amine-containing nucleophiles, which reconfigures the electronic structure and restores emission. In addition, donor-excited photoinduced electron transfer (d-PeT) enables conjugate acceptors to function as reaction-cleavable fluorescence quenchers for activity-based sensing. Together, these mechanisms establish a modular strategy for translating local chemical reactivity into optical outputs that report not only the presence of a stimulus but also the structural state and pathway of molecular transformation. We trace the evolution of this platform from its initial use in real-time visualization of soft-material synthesis, remodeling, and degradation to thiol-triggered self-propagating cascades, programmable multistate fluorescent switches, and fluorogenic dynamic covalent polymers and vitrimer-like networks. We then discuss its expansion into chemical biology, including position-selective cysteine modification, reversible peptide macrocyclization, cysteine-guided protein-backbone editing, vicinal dithiol labeling, albumin-targeted fluorogenic prodrugs, covalent membrane anchoring for imaging protein aggregation, and global intracellular thiol-redox sensing. These applications demonstrate how related reaction pathways can be adapted across molecular, macromolecular, and cellular length scales while retaining an intrinsically encoded optical response. Across these studies, the central design principle remains constant: fluorescence is not an appended label but a direct consequence of chemical transformation. By integrating reaction, reporting, and function within one scaffold, the indanonalkene platform provides a reaction-encoded optical language connecting small-molecule sensing, adaptive soft materials, protein engineering, and live-cell imaging. This framework offers broader opportunities for designing programmable fluorogenic systems capable of sensing, processing, and responding to chemical information in complex environments.

title: Applications, technical progress, and clinical outcomes of indocyanine green-guided near-infrared fluorescence in pediatric urological surgery: a comprehensive review
authors: Zhongxu Wang; Zheng Fang; Shu Dai; Xiangming Yan; Lei Zhang
abstract: Background Indocyanine green (ICG)-guided near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) imaging is established in adult urological oncology and reconstruction for real-time vascular, lymphatic, and parenchymal margin identification. However, pediatric translation remains fragmented by single-center series, empirical dosing, and non-standardized intraoperative thresholds across ages. Objectives Expanding pediatric minimally invasive, microsurgical, and robotic platforms demand evidence-based optical guidance to navigate infantile anatomy, avoid optical cross-talk, and prevent dosing pitfalls. This systematic review of a decade of evidence synthesizes route-specific dosing, optical mechanisms, outcomes, and limitations. Methods PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (March 2016–March 2026) were searched for peer-reviewed pediatric (0–18 years) intraoperative ICG-NIRF urological studies to narratively synthesize surgical approaches, dosing protocols, routes, and outcomes. Results Forty-three publications were evaluated: 19 clinical cohorts ( N = 369 patient-procedures: n = 302 ICG-guided, n = 67 controls; ∼330 unique children after sequential cohort expansion) and 24 supporting references. Indications included varicocele repair ( n = 155; 125 ICG), acute testicular torsion ( n = 54; 54 ICG), renal tumors ( n = 48; 30 ICG), duplex kidney partial/heminephrectomy and nephrectomy ( n = 41; 31 ICG), ureteral reconstruction/pyeloplasty ( n = 32; 32 ICG), renal cyst deroofing ( n = 15; 6 ICG), proximal hypospadias ( n = 14; 14 ICG), and bladder exstrophy/prostatic utricle excision ( n = 10; 10 ICG). ICG-NIRF demonstrated utility in: (1) lymphatic-sparing laparoscopic/robotic Palomo varicocelectomy (0% hydrocele; 4.2% transient subclinical ultrasound changes) and microsurgical spermatic artery identification (shortening operative time, P = 0.029); (2) ischemic demarcation during partial nephrectomy and cyst deroofing; (3) renal tumor margin delineation via bilitranslocase-mediated “optical inversion’ in Wilms tumor/renal cell carcinoma (vs. hyperfluorescence in malignant rhabdoid tumor) and sentinel lymph node sampling (increasing median nodal yield from 3 to 7, P = 0.009); (4) testicular torsion triage via ABC classification and 2-minute perfusion window [Type A predicts parenchymal preservation (6-month median atrophy index 4.75%); Type B/C1 permit acute gonadal/endocrine salvage with ∼87–88% delayed seminiferous tubular atrophy risk]; and (5) flap/tissue perfusion assessment in proximal hypospadias, bladder exstrophy, and ureteral reconstruction. Intravenous (0.05–1.5 mg/kg), intratesticular (2.5–6.25 mg), and intraparenchymal (5 mg) dosing yielded zero systemic adverse events. Conclusion ICG-NIRF provides safe, radiation-free navigation in pediatric urology, though limited by retrospective single-center designs, protocol heterogeneity, and qualitative visual interpretation. Multicenter prospective trials, standardized dosing guidelines, and AI-integrated quantitative angiography are urgently warranted.

title: Single-Nanoparticle Fluorescence Counting Based on Dual-Color Quantum Dot Aggregates for Heparin Quantification
abstract: In this paper, we present a sensitive single-nanoparticle counting method for heparin detection, which integrates single-nanoparticle fluorescence imaging with dual-color quantum dot (QD) labeling. This approach enables heparin quantification by analyzing the combined red and green fluorescence signals from two specially modified QDs, allowing for the precise quantification of heparin concentration in a sample. Due to the optical diffraction limit (~200 nm), fluorescence microscopy captures the spatial overlap of these two QD signals, which appears as yellow spots and serves as a distinct marker for heparin detection at the single-nanoparticle level. Heparin concentration shows a linear correlation with the aggregation ratio of dual-color QDs over the range of 0.001 to 0.02 U/mL, with a detection limit as low as 5.4 × 10−4 U/mL. Additionally, successful recovery tests in serum validate the accuracy and reliability of this method for potential clinical applications.

title: P05.08.B RAS70 peptide-based fluorescence imaging for intraoperative detection of Hsp70-positive high-grade gliomas and brain metastases
authors: A Nechaeva; A Ulitin; D Sitovskaya; V Olyushin; N Yudintceva; D Bobkov; R Likhomanova; M Shevtsov
abstract: Abstract Background Membrane-bound 70kDa heat shock protein (mHsp70) represents an attractive target for fluorescence-guided neurosurgery due to its selective expression on tumor cell surfaces. We evaluated the RAS70 peptide targeting mHsp70, conjugated to Cy7.5 fluorophore, for epifluorescence detection of malignant gliomas and brain metastases. Material and Methods In this prospective study (Ethics Committee approval No. 11-24, 25.11.2024), 20 adults with newly diagnosed high-grade glioma (HGG, n = 12) or brain metastases (MTS, n = 8) received preoperative 5-ALA (20 mg/kg) three hours prior to surgery. Intraoperatively, 174 specimens were collected from necrotic (NZ), contrast-enhancing (CEZ), and peritumoral (PT) zones. Samples were exposed ex vivo to RAS70-Cy7.5 or control NGL-RGD-Cy7.5 peptide. Epifluorescence imaging (FL400/FL800 modes) with target-to-background ratio (TBR) calculation was performed. mHsp70 presence was confirmed by immunofluorescence. Results From HGG patients, 102 specimens were analyzed (39 CEZ, 34 PZ, 29 NZ); from MTS patients, 72 specimens (24 CEZ, 25 PZ, 23 NZ). Mean fluorescence intensities with RAS70-Cy7.5 showed no significant difference between HGG and MTS in CEZ (7.6 a.u. [4.4-11.4] vs 10.25 a.u. [8.0-14.0], p = 0.11) or PZ (7.1 a.u. [4.2-11.6] vs 6.8 a.u. [5.5-11.5], p = 0.44). Overall TBR values (n = 172) were significantly higher in NZ (19.3 a.u. [14.3-21.3]), PZ (6.8 a.u. [4.7-11.5]), and CEZ (9.0 a.u. [4.8-13.2]) compared to control peptide-treated samples (1.2 a.u. [0.9-1.7], p < 0.0001). Peptide penetration depth at 5 minutes exposure reached 1.25 mm (±0.25 mm). RAS70 demonstrated 100% sensitivity and specificity for detecting peritumoral infiltration with optimal TBR threshold >2.3 a.u. (AUC 1.00, 95% CI 1.00-1.00, p < 0.0001), significantly outperforming 5-ALA in both HGG (AUC 0.69, 95% CI 0.49-0.89; sensitivity 70.0%, specificity 86.4%; optimal threshold >0.35 a.u., p = 0.03) and MTS (AUC 0.72, 95% CI 0.54-0.89; sensitivity 72.0%, specificity 72.7%; optimal threshold >2.5 a.u., p = 0.009). Immunofluorescence confirmed mHsp70-positive tumor cells predominantly in CEZ and PZ. Conclusion RAS70 peptide targeting mHsp70 exhibits high diagnostic accuracy for high-grade glioma and metastases, with superior sensitivity over 5-ALA in detecting peritumoral infiltration, offering potential for improved complete resection and recurrence delay.

title: EP07.08 An intratumoural bioelectronic device for controlled, solid-state chemotherapy in paediatric high-grade glioma
authors: I N Van der Auweraert; G Shaw; J Killilea; E Cuttaz; R Portillo Lara; H Wurdak; R K Mathew; R Green
abstract: Abstract Background Paediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGG) remain a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children. Systemic chemotherapy is severely limited by the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and complete resection is difficult due to tumour infiltration in critical brain regions. Developing devices able to circumvent the BBB would unlock the use of drugs previously limited by permeability, while minimising systemic exposure. A promising approach is a minimally invasive bioelectronic device for intratumoural drug delivery. It consists of a neurosurgical-compatible shunt with the tip coated with a conductive matrix loaded with drugs. Application of an external voltage acts as the “on” switch for drug release, while no voltage leaves the device in an “off”-state. Voltage-controlled release of doxorubicin has been validated in 2D and 3D glioma models, yet the ability to tune drug distribution has remained unevaluated. Translating this device to pHGG requires both clinically relevant drug options and precise control over drug distribution, particularly given the critical brain regions these tumours occupy. This work therefore investigates whether different drugs can be released from the device, and whether advanced stimulation paradigms can be used to control drug distribution for pHGG. Materials and Methods Devices were loaded with doxorubicin, topotecan, or panobinostat. Different stimulation paradigms (continuous DC, pulsed DC) were investigated for a 30-min release in saline to quantify drug concentration. Acute terminal studies were conducted in syngeneic pontine DMG mouse models, with devices stereotactically inserted into the tumour site. A + 2V DC stimulus triggered release for 30 min, while unstimulated devices assessed passive release (0V). The resected brains were imaged by confocal microscopy. Results Voltage-driven release of doxorubicin in saline demonstrated substantially higher release than passive diffusion (approximately 3 µg vs 0.5 µg). Preliminary results showed that pulsed DC improved drug release compared to continuous DC. Equivalent studies are underway for topotecan and panobinostat. In terminal studies, voltage-driven release of doxorubicin produced a circular dispersion of 0.7-1 mm in diameter, while passive release was confined to the insertion site. Conclusion Voltage-driven, solid-state drug release from a bioelectronic device has been demonstrated, with preliminary feasibility of intratumoural delivery confirmed in glioma-bearing mice. Varying stimulation parameters improved control of drug release and distribution, opening the possibility for tailoring treatment to individual tumour characteristics. Next steps, including testing device efficacy in pHGG in vitro models followed by safety and survival studies in vivo, will establish whether this device represents a viable, precise delivery strategy for localised chemotherapy.

title: Cy5.5-labeled NMDAR antibody probe for fluorescence imaging of systemic inflammation and treatment response
authors: Yong Hyun Jeon; Sang Bong Lee
abstract: Abstract Fluorescence imaging agents may support repeated assessment of systemic inflammation and its response to pharmacological treatment. We prepared and evaluated N-Ab-NIR, a Cy5.5-labeled N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antibody conjugate, as a candidate inflammation imaging probe. Probe preparation was examined by separation analysis and optical spectroscopy. Cellular assays assessed viability, nitrite, inflammatory cytokines, and nuclear factor κB promoter activity. Dexamethasone and indomethacin reduced cellular inflammatory readouts without a marked reduction in viability under the tested conditions. In mice challenged with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), whole-body fluorescence was measured at 1, 4, and 24 h after LPS injection, followed by ex vivo organ imaging. Both treatments were associated with lower whole-body fluorescence than the LPS vehicle group, with clearer separation at 4 and 24 h, and lower lung-associated fluorescence at the final time point. These observations support further evaluation of N-Ab-NIR for fluorescence imaging of treatment-associated changes in experimental systemic inflammation. Additional characterization and specificity controls are required to separate target-related accumulation from altered probe distribution and clearance. The findings do not establish diagnostic performance in clinical sepsis.

title: Near-Infrared Emitting Cu(I) Cluster-Based MetalOrganic Frameworks with Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence
Biointerface-Engineered Screen-Printed Electrodes Enable Wild-Type P450 BM3 Bioelectrochemistry for Myristic Acid Sensing
authors: Seongjin Kim; Hyukjoon Gwon; Seungae Lee
abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 enzymes offer substrate-selective recognition of metabolites, but their use in disposable electrochemical devices is limited by inefficient electron transfer at binder-containing printed electrodes and the need for a protein-compatible immobilization layer. Here, we report a screen-printed graphite electrode integrating wild-type P450 BM3 through a complementary biointerface strategy based on Ar plasma treatment and didodecyldimethylammonium bromide (DDAB) modification. Ar plasma treatment reduced the surface contribution of the polymer binder, while DDAB formed a biomimetic layer for enzyme immobilization. Together, these modifications were designed to address distinct limitations of the printed electrode−enzyme interface. Microscopic, spectroscopic, and electrochemical analyses supported successful stepwise surface modification and P450 BM3 immobilization and indicated improved interfacial charge-transfer behavior. Under optimized conditions, the resulting sensor exhibited a sensitivity of 0.185 μA μM−1, a limit of detection of 1.69 μM, and a linear response up to 50 μM. The limit of detection was below reported serum myristic acid concentrations, indicating analytical sensitivity sufficient to motivate subsequent validation in biological matrices. Among the tested fatty acids, including lauric, myristic, and palmitic acids, the largest response was observed for myristic acid, supporting a preferential response consistent with chain-length-dependent behavior. These findings show that complementary engineering of the printed electrode surface and enzyme immobilization layer can facilitate wild-type P450 BM3 bioelectrochemistry in a disposable format. The platform provides a derivatization-free approach to myristic acid sensing and suggests a route toward printed electrochemical sensors for other P450-recognized metabolites.

title: P18.18.B Hydrogel-based therapeutic strategy to stimulate immune cell infiltration and remodel the glioblastoma microenvironment
authors: C Cochois; L Martin; M Dubois; M Pedard; L Picton; C Sabot; V Dulong; M Morel; M Madau; P Gandolfo; H Castel
abstract: Abstract Background Glioblastoma is among the deadliest cancers. Failure in curative strategy is mainly due to a hypoxic and immunosuppressive microenvironment. Our aim is to tackle GB cells through a new angle and remodel the vascular and immune microenvironment. We thus built an hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogel-based strategy engrafted with a chemokine to chemoattract GB cells, promote an anti-tumor response and favor cognitive rehabilitation. Materials and Methods The potential of an HA hydrogel as a therapeutic strategy has been validated in vivo in immunocompetent C57Bl/6 mice following resection of a brain tumor derived from a cerebral xenograft of GL261-GFP cells. An HA hydrogel was developed by incorporating a fluorescent probe capable of detecting cellular invasion when injected into the resection cavity.The therapeutic properties has been tested with the adding of a chemokine into the HA hydrogel, administered intracavitary. The brains were then analyzed by 2D immunohistochemistry. To ensure that our therapeutic strategy restores cognitive functions, we conducted a battery of behavioral tests, including the elevated plus maze, tail suspension test, open field test, and novel object recognition test, to assess anxiety, resignation, spontaneous activity, and long-term memory, respectively, before and after treatment. Results To validate this strategy, a preclinical mouse model of GB, followed by a resection and injection of an HA-hydrogel grafted by an innovative fluorescent probe providing a signal in contact with invasive cells, showed that GB cells, macrophages, and endothelial vascular cells invade the hydrogel. Then, the therapeutic property of the chemokine was studied through the intracavity injection of the HA-hydrogel. This HA-hydrogel promotes the angiogenesis and CD31+ endothelial vessels within the hydrogel and in the cavity margin. In the presence of chemokine, the tumor volume at recurrence was drastically reduced, and immune cells infiltration particularly CD20+ LB and CD8+ LT was found associated with the development of immature HEV MECA79+ structures compared to HA-hydrogel. To evaluate the benefit of this chemokine, behavioral activity of GB bearing mice were evaluated before and after GB cells injection and/or resection and HA-hydrogel/chemokine treatment. We established that GB growth is associated with « depression-like » behavior, sensorimotor deficits and impaired long-term memory. When injected or added in the hydrogel, the chemokine enabled recovery of cognitive functions. Conclusion This promising strategy based on a locally attraction of B cells and cytotoxic T cells allows the microenvironment remodeling and thus represents a new treatment opportunity for GB patients. title: Needle in a haystack: Fluorescence-guided 3D targeting for FIB milling in high-pressure-frozen samples
authors: Oliwia Koczy; Fergus Tollervey; Zhengyi Yang; Anastasiia Babenko; Cristina Paulino; Simone Mattei
abstract: Rare subcellular structures are difficult to retain during lamella preparation for cryo-electron tomography, particularly in high-pressure-frozen specimens. Here we introduce two complementary workflows for three-dimensional fluorescence-guided milling on a commercial cryo-focused ion beam-scanning electron microscope with integrated fluorescence imaging. Iterative fluorescence correlation uses repeated rounds of imaging and milling to refine the target position, whereas bidirectional fluorescence correlation images a lifted-out block from two orthogonal directions. We validated both by targeting centrosomes in waffle-frozen early Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, each of which occupy approximately 0.007% of the embryo volume. We recovered recognizable centrosomes in 83% and 67% of lamellae examined by transmission electron microscopy, respectively, compared with 25% using a refined, 2D-guided high-throughput SOLIST workflow, run as a benchmark. Neither method requires hardware modification or fluorescent fiducial beads. These workflows provide accessible strategies for targeting rare subcellular structures during lamella preparation, with or without a lift-out hardware.

title: Digitally Controlled Electrohydrodynamic Nanowire Printing for Intelligent Electronics toward Neuromorphic Systems
authors: Xinxin Du; Yurui Gong; Wentao Xu
abstract: Abstract The digitally controlled electrohydrodynamic (EHD) printing technique has emerged as an important technology for manufacturing advanced electronic materials and smart devices in recent years due to its unique advantages of nanoscale resolution, broad material compatibility, and pattern fabrication capabilities. EHD printing provides an effective approach for constructing highly ordered nanowire structures. With continuous improvements in printing accuracy, manufacturing capacity, and material diversity, EHD nanowire printing is rapidly evolving from a laboratory-scale production technology to a near-commercial level. This spotlight first investigates the printable material systems and preparation processes for the digitally controlled EHD nanowire printing technique. Subsequently, we summarized the latest advancements in the field of digital printing-based nanowire electronics, with the focus on representative applications in neuromorphic devices, nano-masks, polymeric memory, and three-dimensional integrated devices. Finally, this paper examines the ongoing challenges and future opportunities in the aspects of scalable manufacturing, heterogeneous integration, and intelligent bioelectronic systems.
